items.md: The paper asks whether a regional (non-research-intensive) public university makes a local economy more resilient to adverse shocks, chiefly manufacturing decline (p. 1). It contributes in two ways (p. 2). First, it studies resilience, which the university-growth literature had not examined. Second, it proposes a new identification strategy: states placed normal schools (teacher training) and insane asylums in 1830–1930 using similar site-selection criteria, but normal schools grew into regional universities while asylums stayed small. Asylum counties therefore serve as the counterfactual for normal counties. The authors show that a regional university roughly offsets the effect of manufacturing exposure, and they evaluate university spending and bachelor's share as mediators (abstract, p. 1; pp. 13–15). The focus on regional public universities is argued to be policy relevant because they award a large share of U.S. bachelor's degrees (about 21% in 1980; p. 1).

q.exact: We find that a regional university roughly offsets the negative ef- fects of manufacturing exposure. We show the resilience of regional public university spending is an important mechanism, and we show correlations consistent with bachelor’s degree share also playing a mediating role.

items.md: **Identifying assumption.** Asylum counties are a good counterfactual for what normal counties would have been had their normal schools not become regional universities, and asylums have no direct resilience effect (p. 1).

q.exact: This history allows us to identify the effects of universities by comparing the resilience of counties which were assigned normal schools versus counties that were assigned asylums.

items.md: **Estimation.** OLS, reduced form; IV with normal-school assignment as the instrument for having a four-year regional public university is in the appendix (p. 12).

q.exact: As a result, our reduced-form specification will underestimate the resilience effects of a regional public uni- versity. As an alternative specification, we analyze the im- pact of having a four-year regional public university on re- silience, using historical assignment of a normal school as an instrument.

items.md: **Mechanisms.** University spending growth is differentially resilient (Table 4, col. 1). It is about 15% of overall resilience on its own, about 30% with a multiplier of 2, more than one-third once construction spending is considered, and the authors say probably close to half (p. 14). Bachelor's share is higher by roughly 2 percentage points in normal counties (Table 4, col. 2). Descriptive correlations would account for about a third (Rust Belt) and a tenth (2000s) of resilience if read causally (p. 15).

items.md: The identification is a clever but historical selection-on-unobservables argument. The evidence is largely qualitative (Humphreys 1923, Kirkbride's plan, a newspaper account of Kankakee; pp. 3–5) plus balance tests. Balance is good on observed 1840 and 1920 variables, but a few differences remain (Table 1: within 150 miles of the state capital −0.11, p < 0.1; nonocean navigation −0.81, p < 0.05), and 17% of asylum counties also received a normal school (p. 5), which suggests overlapping selection but also contamination. The counterfactual is a county with a different state institution rather than no institution, so the estimate is a university effect relative to an asylum, not relative to nothing. The asylum county still has nearly double the institutionalized population of normal counties in 2010 (p. 5), so the asylum has not been shown to have a zero direct effect.

Pre-trends are only partly addressed. Table 2 shows no differential 1950–1980 growth, and Figure 2a shows the differential effect appearing after 1978, but the design is a continuous-exposure interaction, which identifies the effect of the normal-school/asylum difference only if that difference is orthogonal to manufacturing-share heterogeneity, which cannot be directly tested. Controls for 1950 and 1978/1980 population are included to improve precision. Inference is fragile in the Rust Belt (103 counties, unclustered robust SEs; randomization-inference p-values range from .001 to .102 across columns of Table 3, panel A). The reduced form understates the effect of universities because 9% of normal counties lack one (p. 9), and the authors say the matching alternative gives different results (p. 12).

The mechanism section is explicitly suggestive. Spending's share relies on borrowed multipliers (1.25 to 5 or more), and the bachelor's-share evidence is correlational because sequential ignorability is unlikely (p. 14). The effect is also external-validity limited: the shocks did not directly hurt universities (fn. 7, p. 2).

For the reader's project, the paper transfers partly. The within-state "similar institution" comparison, the exposure-by-treatment interaction, and the event study are reusable for 2-year colleges, and Table 2 shows normal and asylum counties do not differ in two-year colleges (−0.22, SE 0.31). But the treatment here is four-year regional universities with enrollment above 10% of county population, outcomes are employment, earnings and population rather than firms, industry mix or patents, and the identifying history (normal schools becoming universities) has no counterpart for community colleges. Firm and patent outcomes would need different data.
Authors call for work on whether regional universities matter because they are public or because they are large relative to population (p. 16).
Intensive-margin question: whether expanding existing universities has similar effects and whether there are returns to scale (p. 16).
Other plausible channels left for future work: innovation, entrepreneurship, amenities, agglomeration and industrial growth (p. 13).
No causal estimate of bachelor's share on resilience exists in the literature they cite (p. 16).
Resilience to shocks that hit universities directly is not covered (fn. 7, p. 2).

For a study of community college openings, this paper provides a template for a within-state comparison with a "consolation" institution, an exposure-by-treatment interaction to detect resilience rather than average growth, and an event-study check for pre-existing differences. It also shows that mechanisms (institutional spending, education levels) can be probed with mediation logic while being honest about sequential ignorability. It does not provide firm, industry-mix or patent outcomes, and the treatment is large four-year universities. A 2-year college design should seek openings with documented runner-up or alternative-institution sites, measure firm outcomes directly, and test whether any effect is stronger in manufacturing-exposed counties.
